A_target.statement:
Let $A, B$ be [[Definition:Polynomial over Ring|polynomials]] of degree at most $n$ over $\C$.
Then the coefficients of $A B$ can be computed in $\map \OO {n \log n}$ arithmetic operations.

B_source.statement: The [[Definition:Discrete Fourier Transform|discrete Fourier transform]] of length $N$, evaluating a polynomial of degree less than $N$ at all $N$th [[Definition:Complex Root of Unity|roots of unity]], can be computed in $\map \OO {N \log N}$ operations by the [[Fast Fourier Transform]].

substitutions.the transform being computed: evaluation of each polynomial at the roots of unity
substitutions.the inverse transform: interpolation from values back to coefficients

derived.the convolution of coefficient sequences: the coefficients of the product polynomial
derived.the total cost: two transforms, a linear pointwise pass, and one inverse transform

object_map.reformulation: Move to the evaluation representation, where multiplying polynomials becomes multiplying vectors pointwise.

validity_conditions: The product of two polynomials evaluated at a point is the product of their values, so multiplication becomes pointwise in the evaluation representation.
The transform length must be at least the degree of the product, so both inputs are padded to avoid wraparound of the cyclic convolution.
The ground ring must contain suitable roots of unity and an inverse of the transform length; over rings lacking them one works in an extension or uses a number-theoretic transform.
proof_plan: Pad both coefficient sequences with zeros to length $N$, a power of $2$ with $N > 2 n$.

Using the [[Fast Fourier Transform]], compute:
:$\map A {\omega^k}, \map B {\omega^k}$ for $k = 0, \ldots, N - 1$
where $\omega = e^{2 \pi i / N}$.

Multiply pointwise in $\map \OO N$ operations:
:$\map {\paren {A B} } {\omega^k} = \map A {\omega^k} \map B {\omega^k}$
